blocks.text: Code is written once but history is read many times: during review, when bisecting a regression, when deciding whether a change is safe to revert, and when generating release notes. A history of small, well-described commits is a debugging tool. A history of "wip", "fix" and "more changes" is noise.

blocks.code:
Fix double charge when payment webhook is retried

Stripe retries webhooks if we respond slower than 10s. The handler
created a new charge record on every delivery, so a slow database
could charge a customer twice.

Store the Stripe event ID with a unique constraint and ignore
duplicate deliveries.

Fixes #412

items: Separate the subject from the body with a blank line.
Keep the subject to about 50 characters (hard limit around 72).
Capitalize the subject and do not end it with a period.
Use the imperative mood: "Fix bug", not "Fixed bug" or "Fixes bug". A good subject completes the sentence "If applied, this commit will...".
Wrap the body at about 72 characters.
Explain what and why in the body; the diff already shows how.
Reference issues or tickets in the footer (Fixes #412 closes the issue on GitHub when merged into the default branch).

blocks.text: Many teams adopt the Conventional Commits format, a machine-readable convention that lets tools generate changelogs and choose version bumps automatically. You will use it for release automation in Module 7.

blocks.code:
<type>(<optional scope>): <description>

feat(api): add stock level endpoint
fix(auth): reject expired refresh tokens
docs: document local setup with Docker
refactor(orders)!: rename total() to grand_total()

BREAKING CHANGE: total() has been removed.

rows: docs, style, refactor, perf, test, build, ci, chore
! after type, or BREAKING CHANGE: footer

blocks.text: An atomic commit contains exactly one logical change, complete enough that the project builds and tests pass at that commit. It is not about size: a large mechanical rename can be atomic, while a ten-line commit mixing a bug fix with formatting changes is not.

rows: Reviewers evaluate one idea at a time
Reverting one change does not also undo unrelated work
Each commit builds, so bisect can test every step and pinpoint the culprit
A fix can be ported to a release branch without dragging along other changes
git blame leads to a commit whose message explains that line

items: One huge commit at the end of the day mixing features, fixes and formatting.
Commits that break the build in the middle of a series.
Committing formatter changes together with logic changes: reviewers cannot see the real change.

blocks.text: Local messy commits are fine as long as you clean them up before sharing. Use git add -p to split work, git commit --amend for the last commit, and git commit --fixup <sha> followed by git rebase -i --autosquash to fold corrections into earlier commits. Interactive rebase is covered in Module 2.
